title: Gemcitabine and Cisplatin induced posterior reversible encephalopathy syndrome: A case report with review of literature
journal: Journal of Research in Pharmacy Practice
case_prompt: A 40-year-old woman with newly diagnosed stage IV gallbladder adenocarcinoma metastatic to the liver received four cycles of intravenous gemcitabine and cisplatin. Ten days after the fourth cycle, she presented with convulsions and altered mental status. On admission, she was normotensive; serum electrolytes were normal, and renal function tests were deranged. On hospital day 2, she developed aphasia and bilateral lower limb weakness. Magnetic resonance imaging of the brain showed T2/fluid-attenuated inversion recovery hyperintense signal involving the gyri of both parieto-occipital lobes and the subcortical white matter of the right parietal lobe, with abnormal contrast enhancement and a glutamine peak on spectroscopy.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Chemotherapy-related multifocal demyelination syndrome — “Differential diagnosis includes chemotherapy-related multifocal demyelination syndrome, cancer metastasis, cerebrovascular accident, venous thrombosis, and paraneoplastic demyelinating syndromes. Most of these conditions can be easily differentiated from PRES as they are irreversible with distinct imaging patterns on MRI.”  
2. Cancer metastasis — “Differential diagnosis includes chemotherapy-related multifocal demyelination syndrome, cancer metastasis, cerebrovascular accident, venous thrombosis, and paraneoplastic demyelinating syndromes. Most of these conditions can be easily differentiated from PRES as they are irreversible with distinct imaging patterns on MRI.”  
3. Cerebrovascular accident — “Differential diagnosis includes chemotherapy-related multifocal demyelination syndrome, cancer metastasis, cerebrovascular accident, venous thrombosis, and paraneoplastic demyelinating syndromes. Most of these conditions can be easily differentiated from PRES as they are irreversible with distinct imaging patterns on MRI.”  
4. Venous thrombosis — “Differential diagnosis includes chemotherapy-related multifocal demyelination syndrome, cancer metastasis, cerebrovascular accident, venous thrombosis, and paraneoplastic demyelinating syndromes. Most of these conditions can be easily differentiated from PRES as they are irreversible with distinct imaging patterns on MRI.”  
5. Paraneoplastic demyelinating syndromes — “Differential diagnosis includes chemotherapy-related multifocal demyelination syndrome, cancer metastasis, cerebrovascular accident, venous thrombosis, and paraneoplastic demyelinating syndromes. Most of these conditions can be easily differentiated from PRES as they are irreversible with distinct imaging patterns on MRI.”  
6. Radiation necrosis — “Radiation necrosis can lead to widespread white matter abnormalities, cytotoxic edema, which causes true diffusion restriction on MRI and not vasogenic edema, which is typically seen in PRES.”  
7. Acute cerebral ischemia — “Unilateral, systematically arranged lesions with a decreased diffusion coefficient that points to a cytotoxic edema.”  
8. Pontine encephalopathies related to metabolic disorders or mitochondrial encephalomyopathy — “Lesions are localized to the brain stem, and the apparent diffusion coefficient is raised.”  
9. Acute disseminated encephalomyelitis — “This condition has a distinctive clinical context, often following a viral infection or vaccination. There is often lesion enhancement, which may be nodular or ring-shaped.”  
10. Creutzfeldt–Jakob disease — “Lesions with a raised diffusion coefficient, affecting the basal ganglia and the cerebral cortex.”  
11. Gliomatosis cerebri — “Spectroscopy demonstrates a tumor-type profile with marked elevation of myo-inositol.”  
12. Progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy — “There may be single or multiple lesions, which may be unilateral or bilateral and asymmetrical, involving predominantly the subcortical white matter (short fibers) or the parietal and occipital regions.”
